topic: What if all Earth's continents joined into one giant landmass?
scientific_scope_note: The joined map is a schematic, Pangaea-like fit of today's continents (Africa and Eurasia held fixed, drift sped up by millions of times), not a reconstruction of any past or future geography. Pangaea's break-up about 200 million years ago, the South America–Africa coastline fit and plate speeds comparable to fingernail growth are established (USGS). The desert interior, monsoon-lashed coasts and hot-day/freezing-night interior follow reconstructions of Pangaea's climate and basic continentality; that most people would live on the coasts is a plausible inference. The wildlife figures come from research on the Great American Biotic Interchange (STRI): almost half of living South American mammals descend from North American immigrants. Less coastline and fewer shallow reef seas is derived; coral depth limits are from NOAA. The 8–16% livable-land figure is one University of Bristol–led model of the next supercontinent, Pangea Ultima, roughly 250 million years from now.

youtube_shorts.title: What if all Earth’s continents joined into one supercontinent?
youtube_shorts.description:
Push every continent together and Earth becomes one giant landmass. It has happened before: Pangaea held nearly all land until it began splitting about 200 million years ago, and South America and Africa still fit like puzzle pieces. Plates move about as fast as fingernails grow.

In this 3D science what-if, one landmass changes the weather. About 90% of the moisture in the air evaporates from the sea, so a supercontinent's heart would turn into a vast desert, with scorching days and freezing nights, while people crowd onto rainy, monsoon-battered coasts. Animals from every continent would meet, and not all would survive: when North and South America joined, many South American mammals died out, and almost half of living South American mammals descend from northern immigrants. At sea, less coastline means fewer shallow, sunlit waters where coral reefs grow. And the next supercontinent may be brutal: one model of Pangea Ultima, about 250 million years away, finds only 8–16% of its land livable for mammals.

The joined map is schematic (sped up, not an exact reconstruction); the climate scenes are illustrative.
Sources: USGS (This Dynamic Earth; plate speeds; Water Science School); NOAA Ocean Service; Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute via ScienceDaily; University of Bristol; Florida Atlantic University NASA education module.

instagram_reels.caption: What if every continent joined into one? 🌍 You wouldn’t get paradise: you’d get a desert heart thousands of kilometres from the sea, coasts hammered by monsoons, nights that freeze after days that scorch, and wildlife from everywhere competing at once. Earth has done this before (hello, Pangaea), and South America still fits into Africa like a puzzle piece. The plates are moving right now, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

facebook_reels.title: What if the continents joined again? Earth had one giant continent before
facebook_reels.description: About 200 million years ago nearly all land was joined in Pangaea. If today's continents merged again, the interior would dry into a vast desert with extreme heat by day and cold at night, people would cluster on wet, monsoon-lashed coasts, many species would be lost as animals from every continent mixed, and shrinking coastlines would leave less room for coral reefs. One model of the next supercontinent, about 250 million years away, finds only 8–16% of its land livable for mammals.
